Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): title, DOI and figure captions only
pages_convention: Printed journal pages (p. 1 to p. 15) for body and abstract text, because the supplied jats_text file contains only figure captions and no body paragraphs. Caption locators are cited exactly as printed in the XML text (e.g. Fig. 18). Steps read off figure content cite the figure with the PDF page (e.g. Fig. 19 (p. 13)).

entry.evidence: The timing and relationships between the Sn-W mineralization and associated granitic magmatism in this area have not been well understood.

sequences.source_document: Nguyen et al. 2022, Ore Geology Reviews 142, 104727 (published PDF)

steps.action: The authors take from prior studies the wide spread of crystallization ages for the PiaOac granites, obtained by several dating methods.
steps.quote: the PiaOac granites have yielded a large range of crystallization ages varying from 94 Ma to 82 Ma

steps.action: They ask whether the age span means a long magmatic history, multi-stage magmatism, or incorrect dating, and note that the mineralization age and the granite-ore link are unconstrained.
steps.quote: Does this span imply a long magmatic history, multi-stage magmatism or incorrect dating results?

steps.action: They take from the literature the rival tectonic settings: Nanling-type Pacific subduction or post-subduction versus the Neo-Tethys regime.
steps.quote: Other scholars have proposed that they are probably related to the tectonic regime of the Neo-Tethys Ocean

steps.action: They describe the field geology and petrography of granites, greisens and ore veins at the Lung Muoi and Alexandra deposits, and divide the ore paragenesis into five stages.
steps.quote: Ore-forming processes in the PiaOac area can be divided into 5 stages on the basis of mineral assemblages and reactions

steps.action: They establish from CL images that the zircons are magmatic, then date zircons from six samples by LA-ICPMS U-Pb, keeping only concordant grains (>90%), and obtain weighted mean ages of 88.2 to 88.9 Ma; two Triassic grains are read as captured from the rhyolite wall rock.
steps.quote: indicating that the PiaOac granites were formed in Late Cretaceous time (89–88 Ma)

steps.action: They measure zircon Hf isotopes on 54 grains: homogeneous compositions in the granites, and lower, more variable values in the greisenized granites and the greisen.
steps.quote: zircons from three granite samples have relatively homogeneous Hf isotopic compositions

steps.action: They date cassiterite from three quartz-vein samples in two deposits by LA-ICPMS U-Pb, using only grains with concordance >90%, and obtain weighted mean ages of 88.6 to 88.9 Ma.
steps.quote: The weighted mean ages of three samples are 88.8 ± 0.7 Ma, 88.6 ± 0.9 Ma and 88.9 ± 0.9 Ma respectively

steps.action: They check the cassiterite weighted mean ages against lower-intercept ages calculated from all grains, including the discordant ones (Fig. 9).
steps.quote: [...] lower intercept ages

steps.action: They compare the cassiterite mineralization ages between the two deposits and with the zircon ages of the granite and greisen, and find them coeval.
steps.quote: These data suggest that Sn mineralization in the two deposits is coeval (~89 Ma), and comparable to the zircon U-Pb ages

steps.action: They measure whole-rock major and trace elements of fresh, weakly greisenized and strongly greisenized granites and greisens, and record the element changes during greisenization.
steps.quote: showing strongly peraluminous granite features

steps.action: They set their ages against previously published zircon U-Pb, Rb-Sr and Ar-Ar ages of the PiaOac granites, and find agreement with three of the prior studies.
steps.quote: Our data concentrate at 89–88 Ma, similar to dating results of Chen et al. (2014), Roger et al. (2012) and Vladimirov et al. (2012).

steps.action: They recalculate the published Wang et al. (2011) zircon data using only the seven youngest concordant grains, which yields a more precise and younger age.
steps.quote: If the seven youngest concordant zircons are used, a more precise average age (90.4 ± 1.7 Ma) will be obtained with MSWD = 1.5.

steps.action: They explain away the young Rb-Sr isochron age by invoking the lower closure temperature of the Rb-Sr system, so that it is read as a cooling age rather than a crystallization age.
steps.quote: Thus, the 87Rb/86Sr isochron age of 83.5 ± 6.2 Ma probably represents a cooling age.

steps.action: They keep a crystallization age of 90 to 87 Ma for the PiaOac granites and greisens, which implicitly answers the age-span question as dating artefacts rather than a long or multi-stage history.
steps.quote: [...] that the PiaOac granites and greisens most likely formed in the Late Cretaceous (90–87 Ma)

steps.action: They place the samples on peraluminosity and Rb-Th-Y discrimination diagrams, which show S-type characteristics.
steps.quote: akin to S-type granite

steps.action: They reject a highly differentiated I-type origin on the basis of high SiO2, K2O, P2O5, K2O/Na2O and Rb/Sr.
steps.quote: different from those of highly differentiated I type granites

steps.action: They compare Nb/Ta, K/Rb and Zr/Hf ratios with average granite and primitive mantle values, and use the fractionated-granite field of Whalen et al. (1987), to infer strong fractional crystallization.
steps.quote: indicating strong fractional crystallization

steps.action: They compute fractional crystallization vectors for candidate phases (Ba-Sr-Rb-Eu* modelling, Fig. 16) and compare them with the data trends.
steps.quote: Modeling calculations also indicate a clear trend of K-feldspar fractional crystallization

steps.action: They exclude biotite fractionation, because Fe2O3T, MgO and TiO2 increase, and keep K-feldspar fractionation.
steps.quote: rule out fractional crystallization of biotite

steps.action: They infer a late-Paleoproterozoic metasedimentary source by comparing zircon εHf(t) values and two-stage model ages with regional basement rocks, citing published Nd-Sr-O isotopes as further support.
steps.quote: Thus, the PiaOac granites were probably derived from a metasedimentary source with a late Paleoproterozoic model age

steps.action: They use the CaO/Na2O, Rb/Ba and Rb/Sr diagrams of Sylvester (1998) to identify a clay-rich pelitic source.
steps.quote: further suggest a plagioclase- poor and clay-rich pelitic source

steps.action: They keep the genetic link between the Sn-W mineralization and the PiaOac granites, based on coeval ages and highly fractionated geochemistry.
steps.quote: Therefore, the Sn-W mineralization in the PiaOac region is closely related to the PiaOac granites

steps.action: They propose that the enriched and variable zircon Hf isotopes of the greisen record interaction of fluid-rich residual magma with the wall rocks, which changed the redox conditions and favoured Sn-W precipitation.
steps.quote: More enriched Hf-isotope compositions of the greisen are probably caused by strong interaction with wall rocks

steps.action: They compile the ages of Late Cretaceous granites and deposits across SW South China and NE Vietnam (Fig. 18, Table S6) and compare them.
steps.quote: coincident with the 90–81 Ma granites in NE Vietnam

steps.action: They keep the definition of a single Late Cretaceous SWSC-NEV metallogenic belt that includes NE Vietnam.
steps.quote: belongs to the same metallogenic domain, i.e. the Late Cretaceous SWSC-NEV metallogenic belt

steps.action: They reject the view that the belt is a westward extension of the Late Jurassic Nanling W-Sn belt, because the two do not match in space or time.
steps.quote: consequently is not the western extension of the Nanling W-Sn metallogenic belt

steps.action: They compare the belt with the Late Cretaceous magmatism of the southeastern coast that is linked to Paleo-Pacific subduction (rock types, timing, ore types) and with the subduction geometry.
steps.quote: the E-W trend of the SWSC-NEV belt seems inconsistent with the northwestward subduction of the Paleo-Pacific Plate

steps.action: They plot the belt granites on the tectonic discrimination diagrams of Pearce et al. and Harris et al. (Fig. 19).
steps.quote: they mostly fall into the fields of syn- to post-collisional granite

steps.action: They reject direct subduction-related magmatism, both Paleo-Pacific and Neo-Tethys, for the study area: there are no arc granites or mafic rocks, and the area is distant from both subduction zones.
steps.quote: Similarly, there is no conclusive evidence related to the subduction of the Neo-Tethys Ocean in the study area.

steps.action: They keep an intracontinental orogenic setting driven by the combined far-field effect of the Pacific and Tethys regimes.
steps.quote: the belt probably resulted from the far-field effect of the Pacific and Tethys tectonic regimes together

No: ages and sources are inferred from U-Pb and Hf isotopes
Constrain the granite and mineralization ages, the petrogenesis and the tectonic setting
Age span: long history, multi-stage magmatism, or dating error; setting: Pacific, Neo-Tethys, or combined
Only qualitatively (arc rocks, belt trend, timing relative to the coast and Nanling)
Found: natural samples of a past event known from traces

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Repeated across six zircon samples, three cassiterite samples from two deposits, and regional intrusions
Ages agree across samples, two chronometers, two age calculations and three prior studies
Granites 90–87 Ma with coeval ~89 Ma mineralization kept; combined far-field setting as best explanation

end.claim: The PiaOac granites crystallized at 90–87 Ma and the associated Sn-W mineralization at ~89 Ma, so the mineralization is closely related to the granitic magmatism.

decisive_move.sentence: LA-ICPMS U-Pb dating of cassiterite from the ore veins gave the first mineralization age (~89 Ma); without it the claimed coevality with the zircon-dated granites would not exist.

gates.evidence: Action: sampling of granite, greisen and cassiterite veins was directed by the stated age-span and timing question (p. 2), not by a stated hypothesis. Claim: coevality could have failed if the cassiterite ages had differed from the zircon ages (p. 8). The tectonic claim faced no test it could fail; it rests on argument by elimination (p. 13). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen; the concordance threshold of >90% is stated without justification of when it was set.

imports.item: LA-ICPMS for U-Pb dating and Hf isotope analysis
cathodoluminescence imaging of zircon and cassiterite

novelty_claims.quote: LA-ICPMS U-Pb dating of cassiterite is used for the first time to determine the mineralization age of the Sn-W deposits
the timing of Sn-W mineralization has not been constrained

limits: The supplied XML text holds only figure captions, so body quotes are located by printed pages. The analytical details (Supporting information S1) and data tables S1–S6 were not supplied, so standards, reference materials and common-Pb corrections cannot be checked. No review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence. The paper does not explain the choice of the >90% concordance cutoff. The age-span question (long, multi-stage, or erroneous) is answered only implicitly, by favouring prior results that agree with the new ages and reinterpreting the rest. Sub-claim statuses: S-type, strongly fractionated petrogenesis from a pelitic metasedimentary source is best_explanation. The granite-ore genetic link is best_explanation, resting on age coincidence and geochemistry. Wall-rock interaction changing the redox state is a hypothesis without a test. The SWSC-NEV belt and its intracontinental far-field Pacific-plus-Tethys setting are best_explanation by elimination, with no crucial test. The combined-regime option was already proposed by Wang et al. (2011), a point the paper itself makes. Inference: the coder treats the comparison with prior ages as a replication check because the independent data are other groups' and the comparison is done here.
